title: Stone Points From Arabia May Have Carried Poison
paragraphs: Some 125,000 years ago, in what is now the Empty Quarter of Saudi Arabia, a freshwater lake drew animals and people alike, and a paper in the journal Science suggests that those who gathered there were more sophisticated hunters than the barren landscape today would imply. The team, drawn from Griffith University, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology and the Saudi Heritage Commission, worked at 'Uruq Aljelibah, where more than 5,000 stone artefacts lay amid the fossils of hippos, buffalo, camels, gazelles and oryx.

Microscopy revealed animal tissue near the tips of several stone points and plant resin and fibres at their bases, a sign that they were hafted onto shafts. Some showed impact fractures consistent with the pursuit of large game, and the tools clustered closely where bones did, hinting that the shore doubled as hunting ground and butchery. "This suggests people were manufacturing composite weapons made from multiple materials," said lead researcher Christopher Clarkson.

It is the poison that has captured the imagination, and also the part that most needs a pinch of salt. Chemical markers tied to Acokanthera schimperi, the arrow-poison tree, appeared on several points, which raises the possibility of toxic weapons; yet poison use is inferred, not demonstrated, and the release offers no counts, dating details or sample sizes. Until independent work backs it up, the claim belongs among the intriguing hypotheses and not the established facts.

questions.q: What do composite weapons mean in this study?
questions.a: Weapons made from multiple materials, such as stone, resin and fibre.

questions.q: What does the clustering of tools and bones imply?
questions.a: That the lakeshore was both a hunting ground and a place to process animals.

questions.q: What information is missing from the press release?
questions.a: Exact counts, dating details and sample sizes.
